newsitem.title: USA: Blindness among diabetics may be rising needlessly.
newsitem.headline: Blindness among diabetics may be rising needlessly.

text.p: Diabetes is still the leading cause of new blindness among American adults even though such vision loss can be prevented, federal health officials said Thursday.

The U.S. Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said cases of blindness caused by diabetes increased slightly in Massachusetts in 1994. Figures from Massachusetts have been used by officials to estimate national trends because no nationwide statistics are available.

Much of the vision loss caused by diabetes is preventable through regular eye exams, the CDC said. Early detection of diabetic retinopathy, which causes 12,000 to 24,000 new cases of blindness every year, and the use of laser photocoagulation can reduce severe vision loss 50 to 90 percent.
"Only about half of all persons with diabetes are getting the recommended annual eye check," said CDC epidemiologist Dr. Alan Penman.

Diabetes is the leading cause of new cases of blindness among adults 20 to 74 years of age. Diabetes accounts for about eight percent of cases of legal blindness and 12 percent of all new cases of blindness every year.

There were 3,434 cases of blindness caused by diabetes in Massachusetts in 1994, according to a registry maintained by the Massachusetts Commission for the Blind. The yearly average between 1987 and 1994 was 2,994, the CDC said.

The apparent increase may be because "people with diabetes are living longer with their blindness," Penman said. In Massachusetts, between 1987 and 1994, the average length of time people with diabetes lived after they had been diagnosed as blind increased from 6.8 years to 8.7 years.
Government officials had set a goal of reducing the incidence of blindness from diabetes by 50 percent by the year 2,000.

About 16 million people had diabetes in 1995, but only eight million had been diagnosed, the CDC said. Diabetes is the nation's seventh-leading cause of death and can also lead to heart disease, kidney failure and the amputation of feet and legs.
